newsitem.title: USA: World Bank sees solid Argentine, Mexican recovery.
newsitem.headline: World Bank sees solid Argentine, Mexican recovery.

text.p: Argentina and Mexico are poised to post solid economic growth this year after bouncing back from the recent peso crisis, World Bank officials said.
However, domestic consumption in Mexico will take longer to recover due to the effect of the 1995 recession on its homes and companies, they said at a news conference.
For 1997, the World Bank expects Argentina's GDP to increase by five percent and Mexico's by between four and 4.4 percent, the bank's Latin America chief economist, Guillermo Perry, said.

"We are pretty confident that in the case of Argentina we are going to see growth rates of about five percent from this year onwards because the recovery is very balanced," said Perry, a former Colombian finance minister.
Argentina's GDP grew by 4.4 percent last year, compared with a 4.6 percent contraction in 1995.
Perry noted that Argentina had strengthened its banking system, which had been buffeted during the peso crisis.
"Of course, there always are external risks that may have an impact, but in general we are seeing a very solid situation in (the Argentine) recovery," he added.

Mexico's growth rates, on the other hand, would be dampened by the weight of corporate and personal debt incurred during the 1994 credit boom and the fallout effect on the Mexican banking sector, Perry said.
"The (legacy) of the crisis is more profound in Mexico's case, so it's taking more time to work out the problems of indebtedness," he said.

Since consumer growth is only beginning to pick up and banks are just starting to resume loans to the private sector, the World Bank's projections for Mexican GDP growth are more cautious, Perry said, ranging between 4.0 and 4.4 percent.
Mexico's GDP grew by 5.1 percent in 1996, rebounding from a 6.2 percent drop in 1995.
Perry argued that the level of consumer demand Mexico had reached in 1994, stoked by an overvalued peso and easy credit, was unsustainable and therefore a poor point of reference.
"You need a reasonable level of consumer demand, some strength in it, but you really don't want credit booms again," he said.

The World Bank's Latin America and Caribbean department vicepresident, Shahid Javed Burki, said that the recoveries in Argentina and Mexico would help the whole region return this year to the growth rates attained before the peso crisis.
"The two countries that were badly hurt two years ago, Mexico and Argentina, have successfully weathered the storm and are now on their way to recovery," he said.
The recessions in the Argentine and Mexican economies dragged down the whole region's economic growth rate down to 1.3 percent in 1995, the lowest so far this decade.
